questions.question_text: A car travelling on a dry road has a reaction distance of $16$ m and a braking distance of $29$ m. What is the total stopping distance?

options.why: Subtracted the reaction distance from braking distance instead of adding them.
Doubled the braking distance, ignoring the reaction distance component.
Doubled the reaction distance instead of adding reaction and braking distances.

questions.question_text:
A vehicle is travelling at $72$ km/h.
The driver has a reaction time of $1.5$ seconds.
What is the reaction distance?

options.why: Multiplied speed directly by time without converting km/h to m/s.
Converted speed to m/s but forgot to multiply by the reaction time.
Divided speed by reaction time instead of multiplying speed by time.

questions.question_text:
The braking distance of a car is given by $d = 0.01v^2$, where $d$ is in metres and $v$ is speed in km/h.
What is the braking distance when the car is travelling at $70$ km/h?

options.why: Multiplied $0.01$ by $v$ instead of squaring $v$ first.
Used $0.1$ instead of $0.01$ as the formula multiplier.
Equated braking distance directly to speed without using the formula.

questions.question_text: A car travels at $54$ km/h with a driver reaction time of $1.2$ s. Using the braking distance formula $d = 0.01v^2$ ($v$ in km/h), what is the total stopping distance?

options.why: Did not convert km/h to m/s when finding the reaction distance ($54 \times 1.2 + 29.16$).
Calculated the braking distance only and omitted the reaction distance.
Calculated the reaction distance only and omitted the braking distance.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Reaction distance} = \frac{54}{3.6} \times 1.2$
$= 15 \times 1.2$
$= 18\text{ m}$
$\text{Braking distance} = 0.01 \times 54^2$
$= 29.16\text{ m}$
$\text{Stopping distance} = 18 + 29.16$
$= 47.16\text{ m}$

questions.question_text:
A vehicle travels at $90$ km/h.
The driver's reaction time is $1.6$ s, and the braking distance is modelled by $d = \frac{v^2}{150}$ ($v$ in km/h).
What is the total stopping distance?

options.why: Used speed in km/h directly for reaction distance ($90 \times 1.6 + 54$) without dividing by $3.6$.
Calculated only the braking distance component and forgot reaction distance.
Calculated only the reaction distance component and forgot braking distance.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Reaction distance} = \frac{90}{3.6} \times 1.6$
$= 25 \times 1.6$
$= 40\text{ m}$
$\text{Braking distance} = \frac{90^2}{150}$
$= \frac{8100}{150}$
$= 54\text{ m}$
$\text{Stopping distance} = 40 + 54$
$= 94\text{ m}$

questions.question_text:
A vehicle travelling at $108$ km/h takes $78$ m in total to stop.
If the braking distance is $48$ m, what was the driver's reaction time?

options.why: Divided the total stopping distance ($78$ m) by speed in m/s instead of using reaction distance.
Divided reaction distance by speed in km/h ($30 / 108$) instead of converting speed to m/s.
Used the braking distance ($48$ m) instead of reaction distance to find reaction time.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Reaction distance} = 78 - 48$
$= 30\text{ m}$
$\text{Speed in m/s} = \frac{108}{3.6}$
$= 30\text{ m/s}$
$\text{Reaction time} = \frac{30}{30}$
$= 1.0\text{ s}$

questions.question_text:
Two cars travel at $54$ km/h and $72$ km/h respectively.
Both drivers have a reaction time of $1.0$ s and both cars have braking distance $d = 0.01v^2$ ($v$ in km/h).
How much further does the faster car take to stop?

options.why: Compared only the braking distances ($51.84 - 29.16$) and ignored the difference in reaction distances.
Compared only the reaction distances ($20 - 15$) and ignored the difference in braking distances.
Calculated the stopping distance of the faster car without subtracting the slower car's stopping distance.

questions.solution_text:
At $54$ km/h:
$\text{Reaction distance} = \frac{54}{3.6} \times 1.0 = 15\text{ m}$
$\text{Braking distance} = 0.01 \times 54^2 = 29.16\text{ m}$
$\text{Stopping distance} = 15 + 29.16 = 44.16\text{ m}$
At $72$ km/h:
$\text{Reaction distance} = \frac{72}{3.6} \times 1.0 = 20\text{ m}$
$\text{Braking distance} = 0.01 \times 72^2 = 51.84\text{ m}$
$\text{Stopping distance} = 20 + 51.84 = 71.84\text{ m}$
$\text{Difference} = 71.84 - 44.16$
$= 27.68\text{ m}$

questions.question_text: A vehicle travelling at $50$ km/h has a driver reaction time of $0.72$ s and a total stopping distance of $25$ m. If the braking distance formula is $d = kv^2$ (with $v$ in km/h), what is the value of $k$?

options.why: Divided total stopping distance by $v^2$ ($25 / 2500$) without subtracting reaction distance.
Divided reaction distance by $v^2$ ($10 / 2500$) instead of braking distance.
Divided braking distance by $v$ ($15 / 50$) instead of $v^2$ ($2500$).
